title: The mountains sang with Dawud
hook: the mountains and birds echo Dawud's praise, and iron is made soft in his hand (34:10–11)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Al-Ahzab with salawat, and your line was blessings on him. Did you slow down at his name even once? Today, a new surah. Day five hundred forty-three.

Stand in a stone stairwell, or under a highway bridge, and hum one low note. The walls hum it back. Children find this out on their own, and then they do it twice. Surah thirty-four, Saba', opens its stories with a man whose praise did that on a scale no stairwell could manage. He sang, and the hills answered. The birds joined in. And the same hands that held the song could bend iron like clay. His name is Dawud, the David of the Psalms, and today the mountains sing along.

Verse ten. Allah gave Dawud a grace, and then speaks to the landscape. Pickthall: "O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise!" The Arabic verb, awwibi, carries the sense of returning, coming back again and again, the way an echo does. So the hills don't just hear him; they give the praise back. Surah Sad says it too: the mountains glorified with him at nightfall and at sunrise, and the birds gathered. In the Qur'an, Dawud is given the Zabur, a scripture Muslims connect with the Psalms. And there's a hadith that shows how his voice was remembered. When the Prophet ﷺ heard his companion Abu Musa reciting the Qur'an beautifully, he told him he'd been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud. A voice like Dawud's became a way to praise a beautiful reciter. Then verse ten turns: and We made the iron supple for him. Verse eleven tells him to make coats of mail and to measure the links well. The singer is also a smith. And another hadith adds that Dawud ate only from the work of his own hands, though he was a king. Hold those together. The same man lifts praise so beautiful the mountains join, and sits at a workbench getting the rings of armor the right size. The verse ends with an instruction to him and his family: work righteousness. Worship and work, in one pair of hands, and the world around him answering.
screen: `A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAWUD.`

segments.voice: The practice: sing or hum a praise. Sit comfortably. If you're Muslim, or want to try, quietly hum or say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, a few times, letting the sound fill your chest. If that isn't yours, hum one low note and feel where it lands in your body, then in the room. Notice the room giving a little of it back. Then let the sound stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves. The bell holds the time.
Awwibi, the word telling the hills to echo Dawud's praise, again and again, like a returning echo. In Surah Saba', birds join in too, and the iron softens in his hands. Today's word.
Your line: the mountains sang along. Today, do one piece of ordinary work with care, the way Dawud measured his rings, and notice if anything around you answers. Day five hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Dawud as a prophet given the Zabur; beautiful Qur'an recitation is still praised by comparing it to his voice, and many Muslims glorify Allah aloud or quietly with subhanallah throughout the day.

original.note: Arabic: O mountains, echo with him. awwibi carries the sense of returning, again and again.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice image of nature and a singer.
what it means: hills and birds are told to give Dawud's praise back, and the singer is also a smith.
what a scholar hears: awwibi, from the root of returning (a-w-b), pictures the echo; Surah Sad 38:18–19 adds nightfall and sunrise, and Bukhari keeps the 'flute of the family of Dawud' hadith.
recall: a sign, and a verse of the Qur'an
